analysis.one_liner: Puts simple nutrition summaries on the front of food packages and restricts 'natural' and 'healthy' label claims.
analysis.headline: The Food Labeling Modernization Act of 2015 was introduced with 4 cosponsors, all Democrats, sent to a House subcommittee, and never received a vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required packaged foods to carry a standard, easy-to-read nutrition summary on the front of the package, forced companies to disclose how much added sugar, caffeine, and whole grain their products contain, and set rules for marketing terms like 'natural' and 'healthy.' It would have let the FDA disqualify foods high in added sugar from making health claims, added sesame to the list of major allergens that must be labeled, and created a public, searchable database of food label information with fines for companies that fail to file. The bill died in committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary grocery shoppers, especially families trying to limit added sugar and sodium, people with food allergies, and consumers misled by labels like 'made with whole grain' or 'natural' on heavily processed foods. The bill required companies to back up health claims with documentation and gave the FDA power to police those claims.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a single, standard, easy-to-understand front-of-package symbol showing calories and nutrients of public health concern, in a consistent and prominent location across all products.

Forces disclosure of added sugars in teaspoons and grams, the percent of daily calories a serving provides, the percentage of whole grains in products marketed as 'multigrain' or 'made with whole grain,' and the amount of caffeine per serving.
Lets the FDA require manufacturers to substantiate health claims within 90 days of a request, and sets an added-sugar threshold above which a food loses the right to make health claims on its label.

Requires the FDA to regulate use of the term 'natural,' bars foods above 10% of the daily added-sugar value from being labeled 'healthy,' and requires foods marketed as grain-based to be at least half whole grain to qualify as 'healthy.'
Adds sesame to the list of major food allergens that must be disclosed, and requires allergen information on signs next to unpackaged foods sold at retail.
Creates a public, searchable FDA database of food label information, with civil penalties up to $10,000 per day for companies that knowingly fail to submit it.

analysis.who_pays: Packaged food and beverage manufacturers, who would have faced label redesign, claim-substantiation requirements, restrictions on 'natural' and 'healthy' marketing, and filing penalties. Some compliance costs would likely have been passed on to shoppers in slightly higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on manufacturers, including civil penalties up to $10,000 per day for failure to submit label information, and smaller producers have less capacity to absorb redesign and filing costs.

The bill's definition of 'artificial' is broad, sweeping in common ingredients like corn syrup and cocoa processed with alkali, which industry would have contested and which could have complicated many product labels.

Most of the bill's benefits depend on FDA rulemaking deadlines of two to three years, and the text allows proposed rules to become final only if the agency misses those deadlines, so implementation would have been slow.

Front-of-package labeling informs shoppers but does not by itself change what companies sell or what people can afford; the bill relies on disclosure rather than any direct limits on product contents.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to consumers are real but modest in kind: clearer labels, fewer misleading claims, and better information for people with allergies. The main costs are compliance burdens on the food industry, much of which would be passed through in small price increases. The trade-off is reasonable on its face, and the bill is a disclosure-based approach rather than a heavy-handed one, though its effectiveness depends heavily on how the FDA would have written the rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on November 18, 2015, joined by Rep. Rosa DeLauro, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Two days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, which is where action ended.
The bill had 4 cosponsors, all Democrats.
No further action was taken before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, so the bill never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Packaged food and beverage makers are better off: no new labeling mandates, no added-sugar disqualification from health claims, and no federal definition restricting how they use terms like 'natural' and 'healthy.' Shoppers got none of the improved labels.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.role: Sponsor; ranking member relevant to food and drug policy on Energy and Commerce
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Joined Pallone in introducing the bill.

against.name: Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee that received the bill (114th Congress, Republican-controlled)
against.what_they_did: The committee received the bill on referral and never scheduled it for a markup or floor vote; after a routine referral to the Health Subcommittee on November 20, 2015, no action was taken for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters (the sponsor and four cosponsors) were Democrats, and the Republican-led Energy and Commerce Committee took no action on the bill after referral.

industries.note: The bill would have forced front-of-package nutrition summaries, added-sugar and caffeine disclosure, and substantiation of health claims, and would have restricted marketing terms like 'natural' and 'healthy' that let processed foods appear better for you than they are. That cost is the price of information shoppers currently do not get.

industries.industry: Bakeries, delis, and other retailers of unpackaged foods
industries.note: The bill required signs adjacent to nonpackaged foods disclosing major allergens, a modest compliance cost that mainly serves allergy sufferers buying fresh or bulk foods.

industries.industry: Food label printing and packaging suppliers
industries.note: Mandatory redesign of nutrition facts panels and front-of-package labels would have created work for packaging and label producers, though this is incidental to the bill's purpose.
